texts: good. the coming, its past tense, the 'first' ordinal, the hard-frost kind and both date terms are all carried. The one caveat is not fixable by rewriting: day 92 is stored in the same day slot a day-of-month would use, because the calendar vocabulary has no day-of-year term.

mixed: all the content is there (harbor, white, rime, morning, past), but 'with rime' is filed as the *means the state was performed by* — a wrong fit for an agentless whiteness state, which performs nothing by means of anything; the plain 'with' link on the reified state is the compliant form. If you want a phrasing that sidesteps the adjective-plus-PP shape altogether, write 'Rime covered the harbor in the morning, and the harbor was white.'

good. the wind's coldness, the blowing with the sea as its source, the dusk-to-dawn interval and the past tense are all carried, and the non-volitional wind correctly takes the undergoer role rather than being made a doer.

bad: only one collective adding event is recorded, for the keepers as a body — adding is a per-person act, so the parse also owes a rule handing the adding to each keeper, and without it a keeper you name later inherits nothing from this sentence. Write 'Each of the keepers on the Cliff Path added salt-bloom to the mire-essence in winter.' — the explicit universal forces the per-member rule. (Separately, 'in winter' has no structured calendar term behind it and is kept as a bare time symbol; that is the best available and needs no rewrite.)

bad: two problems. The rule's conclusion carries no past tense, so it reads as a standing habit of Cliff Path lanterns rather than the past fact you stated; and 'salt-bloomed' lemmatizes onto the very same symbol as the substance 'salt-bloom' from the previous sentence, whose mandatory genus then makes every salt-blooming *event* come out as a kind of bloom. Both disappear if you use a plain verb with a lemma of its own: 'Every lantern on the Cliff Path was treated with salt-bloom.'

bad: 'of the Cliff Path' becomes an opaque possession link on a *group* of lanterns, while both 'every lantern on the Cliff Path' rules key on the locative 'on' applied to each lantern — so neither rule can ever reach the lanterns this sentence introduces, and the passage's two halves stay disconnected. Quantify it the way those sentences do: 'At night, the cold wind struck every lantern on the Cliff Path.' — dropping 'salt-bloomed' costs the passage nothing, since the previous sentence already establishes it, and kept here it only adds a property the rules have no way to derive.
good. the burning, the slow manner and the past tense are all carried, and the mire-essence correctly reuses the symbol introduced earlier in the passage rather than minting a second one.

good. parses as a fireable rule, with the stayed-lit state reified, the dusk-to-dawn interval, the continuation marker and the past tense all inside the conclusion, plus the flat 'was lit' form beside it.
